Estimate the health your climate spending buys

The Climate Health Ledger Project (CHLP) tool turns what an implementer already knows into a cost per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) averted, with a range. It should take about 30 minutes.

Nothing you type here is stored or sent. To share your entry, copy it at the foot of the page and send it to richmond@climatehealthledger.org. To carry on later, keep that copy and paste it back into the page. If you are taking part in CHLP's open beta, send your entry to the same address when you finish. That alone does not put it in CHLP's database: your answers on consent decide that.

First: your permission

CHLP needs your explicit permission, so the rest of the page opens once each of these three questions has an answer. You can change an answer at any time before you send your entry. Only you can give consent: a funder cannot send your entry or consent for you. Nothing is sent from this page.

Entries shared with CHLP are open to anyone. Until its database is online, CHLP sends them on request. CHLP keeps the entry as it was received, with its date. If you answer No, CHLP reads your feedback and keeps no copy of your entry.
A check compares four things with your records. They are the units delivered, the spending, the basis for the share that would have happened anyway, and the fit of the intervention and setting to the factors. Your consent covers the result whatever it shows. You see the result 30 days before it is recorded.
CHLP would ask for your tracker figures, to set your estimate beside what happened.

Possible health effects

Not sure what your program does for health? Tick each question that fits. The tool lists the health effects to look for, harms as well as benefits. If you already know, skip this step.

Possible health effects. Not an estimate. Each one is a prompt to check. A number appears only where the tool has figures or you enter your own.

What your program delivers

An intervention is what your program delivers, counted in a unit you already record. A pathway is one route from that unit to a health outcome in one group of people. An intervention can have more than one pathway.

Pick the one that fits your program. If none fits, choose "Your own intervention" and give your own figures.
GuideWhat is this, and where do I find it?

What it means. The thing your program delivers, counted in a unit you already record: buses put in service, children treated, tons abated.

Where to find it. Your program plan or your grant agreement names what you deliver. Pick the line in the list that matches it.

If you are not sure. Pick the closest one and open "About this intervention" to see what it counts. If none fits, choose "Your own intervention". The questions under "Possible health effects" can also point you to a route.

GuideIn the example: solar-powered oxygen, one hospital.

About this intervention: what it counts, what to enter and its source. Read it before the costs.
For example the same fuel, a similar climate or a similar level of pollution. Name a measurement that would check it. The result is marked as extrapolated.

How much you deliver and what it costs

Give a low, a central and a high figure where you can. A central figure alone also works. Type figures with or without commas; the page adds them. Cells pasted from a spreadsheet fill across. A minimum entry is three things: the intervention, the units delivered a year and the cost. The page fills the rest with defaults and lists them under the result.

GuideWhat is this, and where do I find it?

What it means. How many of that unit your program delivers in one year. The unit is named beside the heading once you pick an intervention.

Where to find it. Delivery logs, purchase records, service registers, or the last report you sent a funder. For a program not yet running, use the planned figure for a year.

If you are not sure. Put your best estimate under Central. Under Low and High, put the lowest and highest figures that would not surprise you. Central alone also works.

GuideIn the example: 54.4 children with low blood oxygen treated a year, as the central figure only.

The life of the equipment, or the period a total cost covers. Needed with a one-time cost or a total.
GuideWhat is this, and where do I find it?

What it means. How long the purchase keeps working, or the period that a total cost covers. The page spreads a one-time cost across these years.

Where to find it. The expected life or warranty of the equipment, or the length of the grant.

If you are not sure. Enter your best estimate. If it differs from the years the intervention's figures assume, the page tells you and uses yours.

GuideIn the example: 10 years.

Leave blank to use the intervention's default.
GuideWhat is this, and where do I find it?

What it means. The part of the benefit that would have come without your program. If half the buses would have been replaced anyway, the share is 50. Zero means none of it would have happened.

Where to find it. The baseline in your proposal, your funder's rule on what counts as additional, or what happened in similar places with no program.

If you are not sure. Leave it blank. The page uses the default for the intervention and lists it under the result.

GuideIn the example: left blank, so the page used the default for the intervention.

How do you have your costs?
Enter only the extra money the program costs. Leave out anything you would have spent without it. If the program saves money, type a minus sign before the figure.
GuideWhat is this, and where do I find it?

What it means. What the program spends above what would have been spent anyway. A one-time cost is paid once, such as purchase and installation. A running cost is paid every year, such as maintenance, power and staff.

Where to find it. Your budget, your invoices, or the financial report for your grant. Count staff and overhead that the program could not run without.

If you are not sure. If you hold only one figure for the whole period, choose "One total for the whole period". Put your best estimate under Central, and a low and a high figure if you can.

GuideIn the example: one total of $30,232 over the 10 years, already discounted, with a low of $19,814 and a high of $44,809.

Emissions (optional)
GuideWhat is this, and where do I find it?

What it means. The change in greenhouse gases your program causes in a year. It fills the climate ledger and does not change the health result.

Where to find it. Fuel receipts and electricity bills, before and after. A fall is a negative number.

If you are not sure. Leave it blank. The climate ledger then reads "Not given".

A reduction is a negative number. Use this, or the fuel and power fields below.

The three ledgers in full: health, climate and animal welfare, each read against the cost
Health and climate read together: the rate, and what it changes

A bridge is an exchange rate: the metric tons of CO2e that must be avoided to avert one DALY. Fewer tons for each DALY gives the climate ledger more weight. The field opens at CHLP's default, and you can change it. The rate is yours as a reader. It is not saved in the entry, and it changes no other figure on the page.

CHLP's default is about 3,060 metric tons for each DALY, set on November 19, 2026. It comes from a published estimate of deaths from each ton of carbon dioxide (Bressler 2021), on a path to about 2.4 degrees Celsius of warming by 2100, with health discounted at 3% a year as elsewhere in the tool. Undiscounted it is about 580. Current policies point to about 2.7 degrees (Climate Action Tracker, November 2026). On a path to about 4.1 degrees the same source gives about 1,460, which is the high-warming case and was CHLP's default until November 19, 2026. The evidence supports a range of about 500 to about 8,200, and on the source's low estimate the bridge adds nothing, so the reading is uncertain. The rate is for carbon dioxide, and is not yet set for methane or other short-lived gases.

Detailed metrics, the program officer's view: the outcomes, the share that would have happened anyway, the multipliers and the funder's line
QuantityBest caseCentral caseWorst case

Health-care and productivity costs avoided: a working figure that CHLP has not assessed. It is new cases of childhood asthma avoided for each electric bus, times a published cost for one case, spread over the years the spending covers at 3%. It comes from a different model from the DALY figure, so the two should not be added.

Every result shows its inputs, sources and factors, so whoever reads it can check it. Entries shared with CHLP are open to anyone.

The full logic: how the result is reached

A sheet of the whole calculation, for checking. Select a cell to see its formula and the cells it reads. Each row names its source and the place in it. Nothing here changes your entry.

A red corner marks a figure that cites a study. Select that cell to open the study at the marked passage. Where the study is not attached, the cell shows the citation and its page instead. Either stays open until you close it.
A purple corner marks a figure with a note only. Select that cell to read the note. Load the example at the top of the page to see both.

The file stays in this browser. It is not stored or sent, and it is gone when you close the page. Your entry keeps its name, the page and your note, so you can attach it again later.

    In the full version, each organization and each funder will have an account, and an entry will go from your account to your funder's. The estimate itself will stay open to anyone with no account.
